title: The Word for Not, and the Word for Sorry

lessons.title: નથી (nathī) — is not
lessons.gloss: is not — the word that turns a sentence over

segments.text: Two things you have had since the first chapters. Say the Gujarati for yes and for no. Then say the little word that means is.
You can agree and you can refuse. What you cannot yet do is say that something is not the case — and until you can, you cannot say you did not understand.
Gujarati does not negate છે by putting a word in front of it. It swaps the whole word out:
છે — is, નથી (nathī) — is not.
That is the entire rule, and it is a rule about one word rather than about sentences: wherever chhe stands, nathī can stand instead.

The two halves are still visible inside it. ન is the old na, "not". The -થી is what is left of અસ્તિ (asti), "is" — the same ancient verb that comes down into English as is and into Latin as est. So nathī is literally not-is, two words that fused so long ago that Gujarati now treats them as one.

segments.instruction: chhe — then nathī. One swap, nothing added.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *chhe* — then *nathī*. One swap, nothing added.]

segments.instruction: chhe / nathī, twice, until the pair is automatic.
segments.source: [YOU CONTRAST: *chhe* / *nathī*, twice, until the pair is automatic.]

segments.instruction: nathī alone, as a flat answer. It is a whole reply.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *nathī* alone, as a flat answer. It is a whole reply.]

segments.text: How does Gujarati say is not? (નથી (nathī) — it replaces chhe rather than joining it.) What two old words are hiding inside it? (na, "not", and asti, "is".) Next: the sentence a learner needs more than any other.

lessons.title: સમજતો નથી (samajto nathī) — I do not understand
lessons.gloss: I do not understand — the most useful sentence a beginner owns

segments.text: One lesson back: the word that replaces chhe. And from the verb chapter, long before this one: the verb to understand.
Put the verb into the form that describes what you are doing, and follow it with the negator:
સમજતો નથી — samajto nathī — "(I) am not understanding".
Gujarati leaves out the હું here, the way English leaves out the subject of don't know. The sentence is complete without it.

One thing to know before you say it. The -તો ending is the masculine form. A woman says સમજતી નથી (samajtī nathī), with -તી. Gujarati marks the speaker's own gender on this verb, so the sentence you use is the one that matches you — the same choice the track's gender chapter set up, arriving now on a sentence you will say every day.

This is the repair sentence. When a conversation runs ahead of you, this is what buys you the next attempt — and a beginner who cannot say it has to leave the conversation instead. It is worth more than any noun in this book.

segments.instruction: samajto nathī — or samajtī nathī, whichever is yours.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *samajto nathī* — or *samajtī nathī*, whichever is yours.]

segments.instruction: it slowly, then at speed. Speed is the point; it has to arrive fast.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: it slowly, then at speed. Speed is the point; it has to arrive fast.]

segments.instruction: nathī alone, then the whole sentence.
segments.source: [YOU CONTRAST: *nathī* alone, then the whole sentence.]

segments.text: Say that you do not understand, in the form that matches you. Which letter changes between the two forms, and what does it mark? (-તો against -તી — the speaker's own gender.)

lessons.title: ફ — the consonant pha
lessons.gloss: the consonant pha — the one letter this chapter has to buy

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on, your eyes, for letter shapes on the page and your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script — meet one form until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Both are already yours. Today adds one shape, and it is the only new letter in this whole run of chapters — everything else ahead is spelled with signs you have had for a long time.

Keep ફ visible beside પ. They are relatives and they are not the same: pa is the plain sound, pha is the same sound with a push of breath behind it. The shape says so too — ફ carries an extra stroke that પ does not.
Set them side by side once and look at the difference rather than at the whole:
પ — pa, ફ — pha.
Finger-trace ફ once, then trace it once in the air. Say pha with the breath audible as your finger finishes.

blocks.title: Writing — guided copy, model in view

segments.text: Keep the model in view and copy ફ (pha) once. Compare it against પ beside it and repair only the stroke that separates them. Do not start a row.
Which of પ and ફ (pha) carries the extra breath, and how does the written shape tell you? (ફ (pha) — it carries the extra stroke.) The next lesson is the word this letter was bought for.
Source: Unicode Gujarati chart.

lessons.title: માફ કરો (māf karo) — excuse me
lessons.gloss: excuse me; forgive me — the apology this book did not have

segments.text: One lesson back, the new letter. And from the very first chapter, the word for thank you.
You have been able to thank someone since page one of this book. You have never been able to apologise to them.
માફ કરો — māf karo — "do forgiveness", that is, forgive me.
માફ is the forgiveness itself, and કરો is do — the polite form you already use for asking. Gujarati does not have a verb "to apologise"; it asks the other person to do the forgiving.
Read the first word slowly. મ and the ા stroke you have had for a long time; ફ (pha) you learned in the last lesson. Three signs, and only one of them was new.

માફ is a traveller. It came from Arabic muāf by way of Persian, on the same road that carried બજાર into the market chapter and કાગળ onto the page two chapters ago. The apology in this book arrived the way the paper did.

Māf karo does two jobs, and the second is the one a traveller needs most. It apologises — and it is also how you get someone's attention before you ask them anything: said to a stranger on the street, it means excuse me, not I have wronged you. One phrase opens the conversation and repairs it.

segments.instruction: māf karo again — this time to stop a stranger and ask something.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *māf karo* again — this time to stop a stranger and ask something.]

segments.instruction: માફ, with the model in view. One copy.
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: **માફ**, with the model in view. One copy.]

segments.text: Say excuse me to a stranger. What does કરો contribute, literally? (Do — you are asking them to do the forgiving.) Which sign in માફ did you learn one lesson ago? (ફ (pha).)

lessons.title: The repair kit, all together
lessons.gloss: the repair kit, scored as one performance

segments.text: No new words. One run through the four things this chapter added, scored as a single performance.
નથી (nathī) — is not, which replaces chhe rather than joining it.
સમજતો / સમજતી નથી (nathī) — I do not understand, in the form that matches you.
ફ (pha) — one new letter, the only one this run of chapters spends.
માફ કરો (māf karo) — excuse me, which both apologises and opens a conversation.

Before this chapter a reader of this book could greet, count, name a hundred things and ask for tea — and had no way at all to say that something was not so, or that they had not followed. The four items above are what a learner reaches for when everything else has failed.

segments.instruction: someone asks you something too fast. Two sentences: stop them, then tell them you did not follow.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: someone asks you something too fast. Two sentences: stop them, then tell them you did not follow.]

segments.instruction: nathī alone, as a flat contradiction.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *nathī* alone, as a flat contradiction.]

segments.instruction: માફ — name its three signs in order, then read the word.
segments.source: [YOU READ: **માફ** — name its three signs in order, then read the word.]

segments.instruction: the whole kit in order — māf karo, samajto nathī, nathī.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the whole kit in order — *māf karo*, *samajto nathī*, *nathī*.]

segments.text: You are lost in a conversation. Say the two sentences that get you out, in the order you would really use them. (Māf karo to stop them, then samajto nathī.) Next chapter: the word for and, which this book has also never had.
